vvi.note: A rational agent picks the action expected to maximise its performance measure. Describe the task with PEAS (Performance, Environment, Actuators, Sensors), then classify the environment: fully/partially observable, deterministic/stochastic, episodic/sequential, static/dynamic, discrete/continuous.

vvi.topic: Uninformed search: BFS, DFS, UCS, DLS and IDDFS
vvi.note: BFS is complete and optimal for unit costs, O(b^d) time and space; DFS is O(bm) space but not optimal; uniform-cost search expands the lowest path cost; iterative deepening combines DFS's memory with BFS's shallow completeness. State completeness, optimality, time and space for each.

A* expands the node with the lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n). It is optimal when h is admissible (never overestimates) and, for graph search, consistent (h(n) ≤ cost(n,n') + h(n')). A* is complete on finite graphs with positive step costs.

Minimax assumes an optimal opponent and backs values up the game tree: MAX takes the maximum, MIN the minimum. Alpha-beta keeps the best MAX value so far (α) and best MIN value (β), pruning a branch when α ≥ β; it returns the same value as minimax but prunes exponentially more on good move ordering.

vvi.topic: Knowledge representation: propositional versus first-order logic
vvi.note: Propositional logic has facts with no structure; first-order logic adds objects, predicates, functions and quantifiers ∀ and ∃. Unification makes two atomic sentences identical by binding variables, and resolution with refutation proves a query by deriving the empty clause.

An expert system separates the knowledge base (facts and rules) from the inference engine (forward chaining from data, backward chaining from a goal) and explains its reasoning through a user interface. MYCIN is the standard medical example; the advantage is captured expertise, the limit is brittle rule maintenance.

vvi.topic: ER model: entities, relationships, cardinality and participation
vvi.note: Draw entities as rectangles, relationships as diamonds, attributes as ellipses and underline the key. Mark 1:1, 1:N or M:N on each edge; a total (double-line) participation means every entity must take part. Convert an M:N relationship into its own table with both primary keys.

1NF removes repeating groups; 2NF removes partial dependency on part of a composite key; 3NF removes transitive dependency on a non-key attribute; BCNF requires every determinant to be a candidate key. Decompose step by step and name the dependency each step removes.

vvi.topic: SQL joins, GROUP BY and HAVING
vvi.note: INNER JOIN keeps matching rows, LEFT/RIGHT keep unmatched rows from one side with NULLs, FULL keeps both. WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after; aggregate with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. Be ready to write the query, not just describe it.

Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not see partial work) and Durability (committed work survives a crash). States: active, partially committed, committed, failed, aborted. Explain each property with the bank-transfer example.

vvi.topic: Concurrency control: two-phase locking and deadlock
vvi.note: 2PL has a growing phase (acquire locks) and a shrinking phase (release), which guarantees conflict serialisability but can deadlock. Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until commit. Deadlock is handled by prevention, avoidance, detection (wait-for graph) or timeout.

Internal nodes hold only keys and pointers; leaves hold keys with record pointers and are linked for range scans. All leaves are at the same depth, so search, insert and delete are O(log n) with high fan-out. Drawing an order-3 tree after inserts is the usual question.

A view is a stored query, used for security and simplification; a materialised view stores its result and must be refreshed. A trigger fires on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to enforce a rule; a stored procedure is called explicitly and can take parameters.

vvi.topic: DFA versus NFA, and subset construction
vvi.note: A DFA has exactly one transition per symbol and state; an NFA may have several, including ε-moves. Every NFA has an equivalent DFA via subset construction, whose states are sets of NFA states; the DFA may have up to 2ⁿ states. Both accept exactly the regular languages.

Build an NFA for each symbol, then combine with ε-transitions: concatenation chains them, union adds a new start with ε to both, and Kleene star loops back with ε. The result has one start and one accepting state; convert to a DFA only if the question asks.

Remove unreachable states, then partition the rest into final and non-final groups and refine while two states in a group go to different groups on some symbol. The quotient automaton is the unique minimal DFA. Show the refinement table, not just the final diagram.

A CFG is (V, Σ, P, S); a leftmost derivation expands the leftmost variable each step, and the parse tree records the same derivation. A grammar is ambiguous if one string has two distinct parse trees; S → S + S | S * S | id is the standard example. Simplify by removing ε, unit and useless productions.

A PDA is an NFA plus a stack, so it recognises exactly the context-free languages. Acceptance is by final state or by empty stack, and the two models are equivalent. For aⁿbⁿ, push a on each a and pop on each b.

vvi.topic: Turing machines and the Church-Turing thesis
vvi.note: A TM has a finite control, a tape that is infinite in one direction and a head that reads, writes and moves L or R. It accepts recursively enumerable languages and halts on recursive ones. The halting problem is undecidable, proved by diagonalisation.

vvi.topic: Pumping lemma for regular and context-free languages
vvi.note: For a regular L there is a pumping length p such that every string of length ≥ p splits as xyz with |xy| ≤ p, |y| ≥ 1 and xyⁱz ∈ L for all i ≥ 0. For CFLs the split is uvwxy with |vwx| ≤ p and uvⁱwxⁱy ∈ L. Use it to prove a language is not regular/CFL by choosing the string and reaching a contradiction.

vvi.topic: SDLC models: waterfall, spiral, prototype and agile
vvi.note: Waterfall is sequential with fixed requirements and late feedback; the spiral model iterates through risk analysis and is suited to large, risky projects; prototyping clarifies unclear requirements; agile delivers small increments with continuous feedback. Compare them on cost, risk, change tolerance and delivery time.

Elicitation (interviews, questionnaires, observation), analysis, specification and validation. An SRS states functional requirements, non-functional requirements and constraints, and must be complete, consistent, unambiguous, verifiable and traceable. List the sections, then give one example requirement of each kind.

Cohesion is how strongly one module's parts belong together — aim for functional cohesion and avoid coincidental. Coupling is how much modules depend on each other — aim for data coupling and avoid content coupling. High cohesion with low coupling is the design goal; give one example of each level.

vvi.topic: Testing levels and black-box versus white-box
vvi.note: Unit → integration → system → acceptance. Black-box tests behaviour from the specification (equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis); white-box tests the code path (statement, branch, path coverage). Regression testing proves a change broke nothing.

Effort = a × (KLOC)^b person-months, with different a and b for organic, semi-detached and embedded projects; duration = c × effort^d. Basic COCOMO uses size alone, intermediate adds cost drivers. State the project category before plugging numbers in.

vvi.topic: DFDs, data dictionary and structure charts
vvi.note: A context diagram shows the system as one process with external entities; level-1 explodes it into processes, data flows, data stores and external entities. Every flow must appear in the data dictionary. A structure chart shows module calls, not data movement over time.
